newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK legislature, dubbed rubber stamp, curbs immigratiON.
newsitem.headline: HK legislature, dubbed rubber stamp, curbs immigratiON.

text.p: Shouts of "dictatorship" and "rubber stamp" marked the opening of Hong Kong's China-appointed legislature on Wednesday as the new government rushed through a bill curbing immigration and attempted to suspend labour laws.
Activists from pro-democracy groups demonstrated outside the old colonial legislature building in central Hong Kong in a "day of mourning" for what they called the death of democracy.

Meanwhile Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa got red carpet treatment and a pledge of non-interference as he inspected the Chinese garrison troops for the first time, and later promised that religious freedom would be protected under Chinese rule.
Britain handed Hong Kong back to Beijing as a special Chinese region on July 1 after 156 years of colonial rule.
The capitalist way of life of its 6.4 million people is supposed to stay unchanged, but the Tung government is already cutting back on democracy and civil rights.

Half of the 60-member pre-handover legislature have been thrown out of their seats. The assembly was disbanded last week and replaced by the 60-member appointed Provisional Legislature that held its first full-fledged session on Wednesday.

At the urging of government, the chamber rammed through on a 45-to-six vote a bill to deport hundreds of children from China who claim right of abode in Hong Kong, but who jumped the queue by entering the territory without waiting for clearance.

More than 400 children have been surrendered to authorities since July 1 on the belief that they have the right of abode under the post-handover constitution because their parents are legally resident in Hong Kong.
The government said the bill was needed to prevent a flood of smuggled children, but human rights activists blasted it.

"Such an abrogation of these children's rights is particularly serious because it sets a precedent...of denying by administrative measures the constitutional rights of the Hong Kong people," a Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor statement said.

The government failed in its bid to rush through a bill suspending laws beefing up workers' rights that were passed in the twilight of British rule, bowing to the Provisional Legislature's demand for more time to study it.
The move had whipped up a whirlwind of polemics.
Activists from the Democratic Party and the Frontier alliance, angry labourers and 10 ousted legislators donned black headbands and played funeral music outside the legislature.
"Oppose the provisional legislature" and "A step back for democracy", they shouted.

Unionist and ousted legislator Lee Cheuk-yan declared a 120-hour hunger strike at the busy Star Ferry commuter pier, and said the government opposition to the labour laws showed it was beholden to business interests.

"It is not really Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong," Lee Cheuk-yan told Reuters, citing Beijing's promise of autonomy following the territory's reversion to China. "It is Hong Kong tycoons ruling Hong Kong."
Tung addressed a world Lutheran congress and pledged to protect religious rights in Hong Kong.
"One of the important freedoms my government will preserve is, of course, the freedom of religion," he told the 900-strong international gathering of the Lutheran church.

While Beijing has in the past suppressed religious groups as subversive and now keeps a close watch on their activities, Tung said freedom of religion was guaranteed by the Basic Law, the mini-constitution that came into effect after the handover.
Tung's promise prompted Lutheran leader Ishmael Noko to say: "I think there is a future for religious freedom."
The head of the People's Liberation Army in Hong Kong, Major-General Liu Zhenwu, told Tung during a visit to the garrison that the army would not meddle.
"We will not interfere in the internal affairs of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR)," Liu said.
"We will not create troubles for the Hong Kong government. We will respect Hong Kong's way of life and the rule of law."
But the mood among Hong Kong democrats is sour.
"I feel very angry that the provisional legislature has no basis in law but now it is Hong Kong's law-making body," said former pro-democracy legislator Szeto Wah.

"We are wearing this black headband to signify a day of mourning for democracy. The provisional legislature meeting here is replacing an elected legislature, and this necessitates a day of mourning," said Democratic Party spokesman Cheung Yin-tin.

One notable protest absentee was Democratic Party leader Martin Lee, who says he is not going near the legislative assembly building again until he wins back his seat -- possibly next May if new elections are held.
